answers.headline: No. From age 14 you must show a valid ID when police ask, so in practice you need to carry it.
answers.summary: Everyone aged 14 and over must show a valid identity document (passport, ID card, driving licence or residence document) when asked by a police officer or certain enforcement officers. Not doing so is an offence.
conditions: From age 14
answers.penalties: A fine of up to the 2nd category (€5,500); in practice a fixed fine.

answers.headline: Technically illegal, but possessing up to 5 grams for personal use isn’t prosecuted.
answers.summary: Possessing cannabis is banned under the Opium Act, but under the official toleration policy (gedoogbeleid) the public prosecutor doesn’t prosecute possession of up to 5 grams for personal use. Coffeeshops may sell up to 5 grams per person per day, only to adults, and in most places only to residents of the Netherlands. Growing and supplying cannabis are not tolerated.
conditions: Up to 5 grams, for personal use
Coffeeshops: adults only, max 5 grams per day, usually residents only
answers.penalties: Above 5 grams police can confiscate it and you can be prosecuted. Up to 30 grams: up to 1 month’s detention or a 2nd category fine (€5,500); more is punished more heavily.
answers.regional_variation: Some cities enforce the residents-only coffeeshop rule more strictly than others. Ten municipalities take part in a regulated-supply experiment.

answers.headline: Yes, if you take part in the call yourself. Secretly recording other people’s conversations is a crime.
answers.summary: Dutch criminal law only bans recording or tapping a conversation or call you’re not part of (and that isn’t meant for you). Recording your own call without saying so isn’t a crime. Sharing or publishing the recording is a separate question and can breach privacy rules.
conditions: You must be a participant in the call
answers.penalties: Recording a call you’re not part of: up to 2 years in prison or a fine of the 4th category (€27,500).

answers.headline: No. Since 1 August 2026 consumers may not buy, keep or set off fireworks, except small category F1 items like sparklers.
answers.summary: A national consumer fireworks ban took effect on 1 August 2026. Only local associations or foundations with an exemption from the mayor may set off fireworks at New Year, between 18:00 on 31 December and 02:00 on 1 January, under strict safety rules. Professional displays by licensed companies continue.
conditions: Allowed: category F1 (e.g. sparklers) all year
Associations with a mayor’s exemption: New Year only, 18:00–02:00
answers.penalties: Fireworks are confiscated and you can be fined; heavy or illegal fireworks are punished more severely.
answers.regional_variation: Mayors decide which local associations get an exemption.

answers.headline: Swearing itself isn’t a crime, but insulting someone is.
answers.summary: General bad language isn’t punished, but deliberately insulting a person, in public, to their face or in writing, is simple insult (eenvoudige belediging). Opinions about matters of public interest that don’t go further than needed aren’t punishable.
answers.penalties: Up to 3 months in prison or a 2nd category fine (€5,500).

answers.headline: No. Theft is a crime in the Netherlands, with up to 4 years in prison.
answers.summary: Taking something that belongs (partly) to someone else, intending to keep it unlawfully, is theft (diefstal). Theft with aggravating circumstances, such as breaking in or using violence, carries higher penalties under the following articles.
answers.penalties: Up to 4 years in prison or a fine of the 4th category (€27,500).

answers.headline: Yes. The law only bans holding a phone or other device while driving.
answers.summary: Drivers of any vehicle, including cyclists, may not hold a mobile phone, tablet or media player while riding or driving. Using it hands-free, for example in a holder or through the car’s system, isn’t banned by this rule, but you must still drive safely.
conditions: Don’t hold the device while the vehicle is moving
answers.penalties: Holding a phone while driving is punished with a fine.
answers.activity: Using a phone hands-free while driving
